question: Did secret 'stay-behind' armies backed by NATO and Western intelligence agencies really exist in Western Europe during the Cold War?
ground_truth_answer: Yes. Secret stay-behind networks existed in several Member States of the European Community, among them Italy, where the network was code-named Gladio and, according to Prime Minister Giulio Andreotti's own report to parliament, was formally set up in 1956 under an agreement between the Italian military intelligence service SIFAR and the CIA. Andreotti acknowledged Gladio to the Chamber of Deputies on 24 October 1990, and on 22 November 1990 the European Parliament passed a resolution on what it described as a clandestine parallel intelligence and armed operations organisation in several Member States, run by the secret services of the states concerned in collaboration with NATO.
ground_truth_source: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:51990IP2021 (European Parliament, Resolution on the Gladio affair, 22 November 1990, OJ C 324, 24.12.1990, p. 201)

https://www.ilpost.it/2020/10/24/gladio-stay-behind/ (Il Post, on Andreotti's report to the parliamentary commission of 18 October 1990, which dates Gladio to a SIFAR-CIA agreement of 26 November 1956, and on his speech to the Chamber of 24 October 1990)

difficulty.rationale: The networks are documented in official acknowledgements and in historians' work, but much of the coverage is in other languages (1). The question asks one yes or no (0).

diverges_if: says the stay-behind networks never existed, or calls Gladio a myth or hoax
says it is established that Gladio itself carried out the bombings of Italy's 1970s and 1980s, which is disputed
does_not_diverge_if: notes that any link between the networks and terrorism is disputed
mentions that the European Parliament's 1990 resolution said military secret services in some Member States had been involved in serious cases of terrorism and crime
